one_line: A numbers-driven guide to local AI hardware: memory bandwidth sets decode speed, active (not total) parameters set speed for MoE models, the model file is not the whole memory bill, and KV cache at long context can outweigh the weights.
summary: The speaker argues that local LLM performance is governed mostly by memory bandwidth during token generation, and by compute during prompt processing, so spec-sheet parameter counts and VRAM figures are misleading. He gives a back-of-envelope ceiling (bandwidth divided by bytes read per token, with real engines reaching roughly 50 to 75 percent of it) and checks it against measured numbers on consumer GPUs, a Mac, and dual-channel RAM. He then covers the fit cliff when layers spill to CPU, quantization (4-bit as the practical knee, with quantization-aware checkpoints helping), and the KV cache, which can grow to several times the model size at 128k context. He cites a large long-context accuracy study and argues that context length hurts accuracy far more than 8-bit weight quantization does. He closes with the economics (cloud wins under about $50/month of API spend, local pays back above a few hundred dollars/month sustained), a capability gap on a software engineering benchmark, and the observation that local agents degrade past roughly 25 to 30 tool calls. Most figures are secondhand citations, and the talk is not sponsored.
speakers: Unnamed host of Kai Explains (not named in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: Token generation is memory-bandwidth bound: tokens per second is roughly bandwidth divided by bytes read per token, and real engines reach about half to three quarters of that ceiling.
key_ideas.detail: Each generated token requires one full pass over the weights, so bandwidth is the bottleneck. Two cards are compared: the older 12 GB card with 360 GB/s writes 42 tok/s versus 34 tok/s for the newer 16 GB card with 288 GB/s. An 8B model at 4-bit (about 5 GB) has a 72 tok/s ceiling on the 360 GB/s card and measures 55 (77 percent). Spec-sheet compute numbers are the wrong primary metric for chat.

key_ideas.idea: Prompt processing is compute bound, so the ranking flips: long prompts favor compute, chat favors bandwidth.
key_ideas.detail: Prompt reading runs in parallel, so the newer card with more compute processes prompts at 1,480 tok/s versus 1,119 for the older card, the reverse of its generation result. The speaker's rule is to buy for compute if you paste huge prompts and for bandwidth if you mostly chat.

key_ideas.idea: For mixture-of-experts models, speed follows active parameters, but total parameters still consume VRAM.
key_ideas.detail: On an RTX 3090, Qwen3 32B dense runs at 35 tok/s while Qwen3 30B MoE runs at 153 tok/s (about 4.5x). Sparse models read only a few experts per token. The catch is that sleeping experts still occupy memory: a 35B-total, 3B-active model is about 20 GB on the card. Sparsity buys speed, not space.

key_ideas.idea: Fit is a cliff, not a slope: spilling layers to CPU collapses throughput, and the last few layers cost the most.
key_ideas.detail: A 14B model runs at 2.9 tok/s fully on CPU and 43 tok/s fully on GPU (15x). With 40 of 48 layers on GPU it drops to 12.5 tok/s, so 83 percent of the model on GPU yields only 29 percent of the speed. The speaker says a miss of about 1 GB can push you off this cliff.

key_ideas.idea: 4-bit is the practical quantization knee; 3-bit and below do real damage, and the damage is uneven across skills.
key_ideas.detail: Quantization uses small blocks with per-block scale factors. The talk cites 4-bit changing the next token about 8 percent of the time versus full precision, 8-bit as effectively free, 6-bit as cheap, and 3-bit as damaging (about 9 points lost on grade-school math but only 0.6 on common sense). 1-bit takes perplexity from about 6 to about 60. Reasoning degrades first. Quantization-aware-trained checkpoints cut the 4-bit penalty by more than half.

key_ideas.idea: The KV cache is the memory surprise: at long context it can be several times the size of the model file, so the 'file 1 to 2 GB under VRAM' rule breaks.
key_ideas.detail: For an 8B model the cache is about 147 KB per token. At 4k context that is about 0.6 GB, but at 128k it is about 19 GB against a 5 GB model file. Budget weights plus cache plus working buffer plus whatever the desktop already uses on the GPU.

key_ideas.idea: Keys and values are not equally fragile, so quantize them asymmetrically; long context costs far more accuracy than 8-bit weights do.
key_ideas.detail: Keys pass through softmax, so their errors spread across positions; values are summed, so their errors stay local. The talk recommends 8-bit keys with 4-bit values (about 60 percent memory saved). Across 172 billion tokens through 35 open models at 32k, 128k and 200k context, median accuracy fell 10.5 points from 32k to 128k. One model fell from 93 to 37 percent at 200k, with its invented-answer rate rising from 7 to 72 percent. 8-bit weights cost under 2 points, while context cost about 20.

key_ideas.idea: For a single user, the serving app matters little; the Mac runtime matters more than the hardware upgrade; the decision is driven by workload and volume.
key_ideas.detail: llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio are within a few tok/s of each other for one request at a time, and vLLM wins only at high concurrency. Ollama moved from llama.cpp to Apple MLX on Mac in March, with prompt processing up 57 percent and generation up 93 percent. Local wins for small, repetitive, private, constant tasks (classification, extraction, summarizing your own files, autocomplete). Past roughly 25 to 30 tool calls, local models lose the thread and redo finished steps.

techniques.name: Back-of-envelope decode speed
techniques.how: Estimate tok/s as memory bandwidth (GB/s) divided by bytes read per token (roughly the quantized model size; for MoE, use active parameters only). Expect about 50 to 75 percent of that in practice. Example: 8B at 4-bit (~5 GB) on 360 GB/s gives a 72 tok/s ceiling and about 55 measured.
techniques.when: Before buying or renting hardware, to compare cards on the metric that governs chat speed rather than TFLOPS or VRAM.

techniques.name: Split the hardware decision by workload
techniques.how: Chat and short generations are bandwidth-limited, so prioritize GB/s. Long-prompt work (pasting large documents) is compute-limited, so prioritize compute throughput for prefill. Measure both prefill tok/s and decode tok/s separately.
techniques.when: When choosing between cards or Macs for a mixed workload where one card has more bandwidth and another has more compute.

techniques.name: Full memory budget (not just the file size)
techniques.how: Total = quantized weights + KV cache at your target context length + working buffer + memory already used by the desktop/display on the GPU. KV cache per token for an 8B model is roughly 147 KB, so multiply by context length. Keep headroom well below the card's VRAM.
techniques.when: Before downloading a model for a long-context use case, instead of the 'file 1 to 2 GB under VRAM' rule of thumb.

techniques.name: Asymmetric KV cache quantization
techniques.how: Quantize keys to 8-bit and values to 4-bit rather than quantizing both to 4-bit. The talk reports about 60 percent of cache memory saved with the smallest accuracy hit. Quantizing keys to 4-bit is the main accuracy hazard.
techniques.when: When the KV cache is what overflows VRAM at long context and you must keep accuracy.

techniques.name: Avoid partial GPU offload for the last layers
techniques.how: Test full-GPU versus partial layer offload and measure tokens per second. Do not leave the last few layers on CPU; the talk shows a 40-of-48-layer split losing most of the speed.
techniques.when: When a model almost fits on the GPU and you are tempted to offload the remainder to system RAM.

techniques.name: Prefer 4-bit or higher with QAT checkpoints; avoid 3-bit and lower for reasoning work
techniques.how: Start with 8-bit or 6-bit if memory allows, use 4-bit as the default knee, and prefer quantization-aware-trained checkpoints when available. Check reasoning-heavy tasks specifically, because math degrades first.
techniques.when: Picking a quant level for a reasoning or coding model on a constrained GPU.

techniques.name: Evaluate on your own task before choosing hardware or quantization
techniques.how: Run the same prompts across quant levels, hardware and temperature settings and compare outputs against full precision. The speaker reports temperature shifting accuracy far more than the hardware (up to 9x), and hardware differences of about 0.5 points.
techniques.when: When deciding whether a local model meets a quality bar for a specific task.

techniques.name: Local versus API break-even check
techniques.how: Estimate monthly API spend. Under roughly $50/month, cloud usually wins. Above a few hundred dollars per month of sustained use, a machine can pay back in under six months. Include electricity and the current street price of the card.
techniques.when: When deciding whether to buy a local GPU for steady workloads.

techniques.name: Cap local agent runs at tool-call budgets
techniques.how: The speaker reports local models losing track past roughly 25 to 30 tool calls, forgetting early results and redoing steps even with context space left. Implied practice: checkpoint or summarize state before about 25 calls and restart with a fresh context rather than letting one run grow.
techniques.when: Running agentic workflows on a local model. This is an inference from the talk's observation, not a tested recipe.

numbers.claim: Old 12 GB card (360 GB/s) generates 42 tok/s vs newer 16 GB card (288 GB/s) at 34 tok/s on the same model
8B model at 4-bit (~5 GB) on a 360 GB/s card: ceiling 72 tok/s, measured 55 (77 percent of ceiling)
Bandwidth to decode speed on one 8B-class model: RTX 3090 (936 GB/s) 115 tok/s; RTX 5090 (1792 GB/s) 200 tok/s
Dual-channel desktop RAM (~96 GB/s) gives about 11 tok/s on a 7B model, about 18x less bandwidth than the top card
Prompt processing: newer card 1,480 tok/s vs older card 1,119 tok/s
Apple M5 Max: 614 GB/s over 128 GB unified memory; a Mac Studio reportedly ran a 671B DeepSeek model at about 17 tok/s, under 200 W
RTX 3090: Qwen3 32B dense 35 tok/s vs Qwen3 30B MoE 153 tok/s (about 4.5x)
Alibaba MoE ships 35B total with 3B active (about 20 GB on a card); Google's 26B model has 3.8B active and runs about like a 4B model
Kimi K3: 2.8 trillion parameters, 1.4 TB of weights, 6,800 Hugging Face likes and 2,850 downloads at time of talk
14B model: CPU-only 2.9 tok/s, GPU-only 43 tok/s (15x)
14B model with 40 of 48 layers on GPU: 12.5 tok/s (83 percent of model on GPU gives 29 percent of GPU-only speed)
32B model at 16-bit is 65.5 GB; quantized it is under 20 GB
4-bit quantization picks a different next token than full precision 8 percent of the time
3-bit quantization costs about 9 points on grade-school math and 0.6 points on common sense; 1-bit raises perplexity from about 6 to about 60
Quantization-aware-trained checkpoints cut the 4-bit penalty by more than half; a 27B model goes from 54 GB to 14 GB
8B model KV cache is about 147 KB per token: about 0.6 GB at 4k context, about 19 GB at 128k (model file is 5 GB)
Keys quantized to 4-bit agree with full-precision answers only 11 percent of the time; 8-bit keys with 4-bit values keep 60 percent of the memory
DeepSeek cache compression: about 70 KB per token instead of 300 KB. Gemma's local/global attention cuts the cache from 60 percent of inference memory to 15 percent

Study of 172 billion tokens across 35 open models at 32k, 128k and 200k context: median accuracy loss from 32k to 128k is 10.5 points; one model fell from 93 to 37 percent at 200k (invented-answer rate 7 to 72 percent); 8-bit weights cost under 2 points
Ollama switching from llama.cpp to Apple MLX on Mac (March): prompt processing +57 percent, generation +93 percent
Across H200, MI300X and Gaudi 2, accuracy on the same task varies by about 0.5 points; temperature changed it by up to 9x more
OpenAI sells 1M input tokens for $0.05; DeepSeek runs a capable model for $0.14 (prices as stated in talk)
US electricity about 18.5 cents per kWh (transcript reads '$0.18.5'), up 6 percent in a year
RTX 5090: $2,000 list price, selling for about $4,300 as memory makers shifted lines to data-center parts
Break-even: under $50/month API spend, cloud wins; above a few hundred dollars per month sustained, a local machine pays for itself in under half a year
Standard software engineering benchmark (not named): best closed model 89, best open-weights model 79
Local models lose the thread past roughly 25 to 30 tool calls
Ollama reports 8.9 million monthly developers, double January, used inside 85 percent of the Fortune 500 by a 14-person team
Open weights took 41 percent of Hugging Face downloads this spring; open models handled close to a third of AI requests on Vercel in June
UK AI Security Institute: open weights 4 to 7 months behind the closed frontier, down from 6 to 10 months a year earlier
Sizing rules of thumb: 8 GB runs a 9B model at 4-bit with real context; 16 GB runs a 12B or 26B sparse model; 24 GB runs a 27B coding model at 25 tok/s on a laptop

hot_takes: Parameter count is nearly meaningless for speed; memory bandwidth and active parameters are the numbers that matter, and the spec sheet's headline figure is the wrong one.
The KV cache, not the model file, decides whether a long-context local setup fits; the speaker says the calculator used before downloading was wrong.
Context length costs far more accuracy than 8-bit weight quantization, so the quantization setting most people argue about barely matters next to context.
Temperature moves accuracy more than hardware choice does, which undercuts hardware-first comparisons.

Most figures are secondhand: citations to studies and vendor claims (Kimi K3 likes and downloads, API prices, the 172B-token study) are paraphrased without links, so treat them as directional. The talk is not sponsored, so the caveat is about sourcing, not commercial bias.
The break-even thresholds ($50/month, a few hundred per month) depend on utilization, electricity and resale value, which the talk does not model.

relevance.why: InferCraft runs vLLM on one RTX 5090 with pluggable KV-cache strategies; this talk's bandwidth ceiling, per-token KV sizing and asymmetric key/value quantization directly bear on those choices, and it reports long-context accuracy loss on 35 models.
relevance.action: Add a per-config KV-cache budget table (weights + KV at target context + buffer) for the 5090 and benchmark asymmetric 8-bit-key / 4-bit-value KV cache against the accuracy loss at 128k before enabling it in InferCraft.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps long Claude Code runs with checkpoint/resume; the talk's claim that local models lose the thread after about 25 to 30 tool calls is relevant only if ProsHarness ever routes a run to a local model.
relevance.action: If a local-model backend is added, use the 25 to 30 tool-call degradation point as a default checkpoint interval and test it on a real run before trusting it.
